Their opponents, Sangal, came into the playoffs from a play-in match following the group stage. Both teams stole each other's map pick before FaZe narrowly avoided an upset loss, winning on Cache thanks to timely multi-kills from Russell "Twistzz" Van Dulken and Jakub "jcobbb" Pietruszewski. Dust2 was the first map and FaZe's pick. Despite going down 0-3, Sangal found their groove in the game to take a 7-5 lead after their CT-side. The close affair continued into the second half, with neither team finding the win in regulation. Overtime saw Sangal steal FaZe's map, taking D2 16-13 and pulling ahead 1-0 in the series. With a potential upset on the cards, Sangal's pick was Nuke. FaZe weren't interested in losing here, though, as they stormed ahead to an 8-4 lead in the stronger defensive half. Led by IGL Twistzz's calling, FaZe put together a great T-side to keep Sangal at arm's length and win the map 13-7, evening up the series. Cache was the setting for the decider, and it was FaZe who once again took a substantial 8-4 lead after the CT-side. Sangal didn't go out quietly, though, as they would tie the game back up at 8-8. It was at this point that Twistzz left his mark on the game, coming up with four huge kills in a Tec-9 buy to stabilize FaZe. Up 11-8, it was jcobbb's turn to go wild; the Polish rifler aced Sangal, winning a 1v2 clutch to all but put the game to bed for FaZe. FaZe will now face PURE tomorrow in the upper bracket semifinals at Roman Imperium Cup IX.

title: Does America need an Article V convention to propose amendments to the Constitution? - Harvard Law School
content: Harvard Law conference weighs never-used path to amend the Constitution Could a never-used provision of the U.S. Constitution give Americans a new way to debate changes to their government? That’s what Harvard Law School Professor Lawrence Lessig asked scholars, legislators, and advocates to consider as he kicked off a two-day conference called VthePeople. Participants in the Oct. 2 and 3 conference considered the unprecedented potential for — and advantages and disadvantages of — changing the U.S. Constitution through a federal convention that could be called under Article V by two-thirds of the states. Lessig also asked participants to consider whether citizen assemblies, composed of ordinary people drawing on their lived experiences, might play a role in the process. “I think the objective of today is to begin to imagine even something more democratically exciting,” said Lessig, the Roy L. Furman Professor of Law and Leadership. “To begin to think about … something different, some better structure that might actually give people even more confidence in what a convention here might be.” Lessig, who founded Equal Citizens, an organization that, among other things, advocates for reform of the Electoral College system, was joined during his opening remarks by Michael Farris, cofounder and senior advisor of the Convention of States Project, which is encouraging states to call a federal convention to propose amendments limiting the power of the federal government. “The founders were very aware that the document they were creating would prove to contain imperfections,” Farris said. “Why did they create the convention process to authorize the states to propose amendments as an alternative to Congress? … This power to curb federal abuses just made sense. The future need for an amendment that would grant additional powers to the federal government would likely come from Congress. But if the federal government needed to be reined in, an amendment of that sort was far more likely to come from the states.” The conference drew more than 30 speakers from across the political spectrum, including both supporters and opponents of an Article V convention. Lessig and another Convention of States Project cofounder, Mark Meckler (who cofounded the Tea Party Patriots), hosted a similar event in 2011. The idea, Lessig said, is to “tee up questions … different ways to imagine us solving what is the core problem we are all here to solve: the problem of bringing our Constitution up to date without relying on five justices of the Supreme Court to do that for us, in a way that respects and reflects and maybe builds on the most important contribution America made to the history of democracy. And that is that citizens ratified the idea of their founding constitutional document. That … needs to happen again now, especially now, given the anxiety and frustration and anger and hope all of us have about this nation.” Among the featured speakers were Harvard Law Professor Jill Lepore, whose latest book “We the People: A History of the U.S. Constitution” argues the Constitution has been effectively unamendable for decades, and Laurence Tribe ’66, the Carl M. Loeb University Professor Emeritus, and a skeptic of a federal constitutional convention. Other speakers included Chris Sununu, the former governor of New Hampshire, David Walker, a former U.S. comptroller general, and people who have participated in similar efforts in other countries. Topics included grassroots Article V advocacy, arguments against a federal convention, and past successful processes. Harvard Law’s Richard M. Re, Fessenden Professor of Law, moderated a discussion on the history and traditions of Article V, which lays out the two ways to amend the Constitution. All 27 ratified amendments have originated in Congress, where a proposed change requires approval from two-thirds of both the U.S. House and the Senate. The second path requires Congress to call a convention for proposing amendments upon applications from two-thirds of state legislatures. In either case, a proposed amendment must be ratified by three-fourths of the states. No Article V convention has ever been called. University of Chicago Law School Professor Farah Peterson pointed out that the Constitution meant something very different at the time of its ratification, not least because the federal government had a far more limited role in people’s everyday lives. “Their Constitution was not ours,” she said. “The way that an American knew that he had a federal government … might be the Post Office. There were powers explicitly granted in the Constitution that could have created a strong national government … but … these were paper powers.” A better comparison for Americans’ current relationship to the Constitution, he said, would have been 18th- and 19th-century Americans’ relationships to their state constitutions which, as Lepore described in her keynote address, have been more easily amended over the centuries. University of San Diego School of Law Professor Michael Rappaport, like many speakers, addressed concerns about “runaway” conventions in which delegates might propose amendments they had not originally set out to consider. But Rappaport argued that the Constitution’s text would constrain what a convention could do. Other speakers pointed out that the subsequent ratification process also could guard against proposals considered too extreme. “The convention cannot decide to meet on its own without a call,” he said. Likewise, “if a convention proposed an amendment contrary to the call … it would be no more constitutional than if the convention decided to meet on its own without a congressional call.” University of Texas School of Law Professor Sanford V. Levinson, currently a visiting professor at Harvard Law, said concerns about the legality of a convention or the amendment process might be secondary in some cases to any threat the country or its people are facing. Today, he argued, that threat comes from the Constitution in its current form — or, perhaps more accurately, from people’s veneration of the document. “I’m an increasingly vociferous critic of the Constitution,” he said. “It constitutes a clear and present danger, even an existential risk to our national survival. … [That’s] why I support the need for a new constitutional convention, in order to engage in the kind of remodeling that I believe is both necessary and proper.” He said the most important lesson from the Declaration of Independence, written 250 years ago, is that “an aroused people have the right to overthrow a completely legal regime.” He quoted from Federalist No. 14, one of many papers written in support of a constitution, in which James Madison praised Americans for not having “a blind veneration for antiquity, for custom, or for names,” and from Alexander Hamilton’s first essay in the series of papers, in which he asked, “whether societies of men are really capable or not of establishing good government from reflection and choice, or whether they are forever destined to depend for their political constitutions on accident and force.” “That is the question before us,” Levinson said. “Are we capable of engaging in the kind of audacious reflection and choice that the framers at their best give us as an example to follow?” In addition to panels and social gatherings, the conference organizers also created an artificial intelligence chatbot trained on Article V scholarship that Lessig invited the public to engage with and use. Harvard Law Dean John C.P. Goldberg welcomed participants and the discussion on “one of our Constitution’s most interesting and under-theorized and under-discussed provisions.” He read a passage from the book “The Framers’ Coup: The Making of the United States Constitution,” by Michael Klarman, Charles Warren Professor of American Legal History, which quoted a Massachusetts delegate saying “great or important change in government had too often been written in blood … if in the course of its operation, this government shall appear to be too severe, [Article V is] the means by which this severity may be attempted and corrected.” “Whether in these challenging times an amendment convention can deliver on this promise is exactly what you have been discussing and will be discussing,” Goldberg said, calling those “fundamental and urgent questions.” Want to stay up to date with Harvard Law Today? title: 'Take Me to Night City' — Smile 2 Star Kyle Gallner Wants to Play V in Paramount’s Live-Action Cyberpunk 2077 Movie - IGN
content: Smile 2 star Kyle Gallner is making it known that he’s ready and willing to play V in Paramount’s live-action film adaptation of Cyberpunk 2077. Cyberpunk 2077 has come a long way from its roots as a tabletop RPG. Thanks to CD Projekt Red’s video game and its standout expansion, as well as the critically-acclaimed Edgerunners spinoff anime from Studio Trigger, fans of the gritty sci-fi series are eating well. They’re about to get fed even more, as Paramount revealed that it is developing a live-action movie based on the franchise. Thus far, we’re not sure of any plot details, so it’s possible that we could follow V’s adventures with Johnny Silverhand, or Idris Elba’s Solomon Reed before he meets V — or heck, maybe even Edgerunner 2’s Weak Kingsley, for all we know! What we do know is that there’s no shortage of possibilities for this film, and that’s what has fans so excited. One of these fans is none other than actor Kyle Gallner, who is raring to step into Night City as the male version of V. Mere hours after Paramount announced the news on October 8, Gallner posted a photo of himself sporting a close-shaved crop of hair, similar to V’s hairstyle in the game’s marketing materials, along with the caption: “Take me to night city.” It’s safe to say that fans are pretty enthusiastic about this possible casting, with many already envisioning Gallner alongside Keanu Reeves’ Johnny Silverhand. “Kyle and Keanu. Sounds outstanding,” one wrote, while another said Gallner would be “PERFECT casting.” “You and Keanu teaming up? I could be on board for that,” another commented. “He’s HIM! Paramount, please consider,” yet another vouched. For now, details about the movie are being kept under wraps, but CDPR co-CEO Michał Nowakowski promised that more information will come soon. "We're excited about Paramount as a future partner who shares our creative ambitions for the Cyberpunk franchise," he said on X. "We look forward to sharing more details at the appropriate time." While they wait for more news, fans can look forward to Edgerunners 2, set to air on Netflix on October 20, 2026. It’s pretty presumptuous to make someone a mixtape. You might like the person. Heck, you might even think you love them. But giving a person a mixtape of all things is also kind of like saying, “Here’s a collection of emotions I’ve decided you should feel, in an order I’ve personally determined, for reasons that probably won’t make sense to anyone but me. Enjoy!” Yikes. The ninth installment in the beloved “V/H/S” franchise takes that potentially awkward premise to a horrifying cinematic extreme, with the new anthology streaming on Shudder October 9. This time, the night’s entertainment includes four short films and a handful of musical interludes, all built around the theme of… sound? A perfectly fine excuse to make another “V/H/S” movie, to be sure. But “V/H/S Mixtape” also suggests the series’ sense of novelty is growing harder to maintain. Broadly speaking, the element of surprise goes hand-in-hand with found footage. “V/H/S” made its comeback in 2021, after the seven-year gap that followed the franchise’s critical low point, “V/H/S: Viral.” Today, the brand’s stewards are a mix of veteran producers and relative newcomers who have kept the fanbase alive by using the IP to platform filmmakers with a remarkable array of creative talents. In “V/H/S Mixtape” (the first installment released under new franchise owners Spooky Pictures and Image Nation Abu Dhabi), the assembled artists are at remarkably different places in their careers, too. Veteran director and Spike Lee collaborator Ernest Dickerson brings decades of filmmaking experience, while French horror director David Moreau arrives fresh off the success of 2024’s “MadS.” Wu-Tang Clan’s RZA and electronic musician Flying Lotus contribute their unique sensibilities as well — with Ghost frontman Tobias Forge making his directorial debut. But it’s emerging animator Renee Zhan who makes the strongest case for the franchise’s continued relevance as a showcase for unconventional horror talent. The boundaries of contemporary found footage are becoming harder to define, and there’s no denying that a vertical video randomly dropped into someone’s feed can trick them in ways a feature film can’t. Against that increasingly unpredictable digital landscape, Zhan’s contribution, “Dance, Dance, Dance, Dance,” is all the more impressive for embracing a decidedly antiquated broadcast format: the children’s puppet show. Featuring original creations from Jim Henson’s Creature Shop, a quick behind-the-scenes look at the long-canceled “Curious Chorus” kids’ program reveals a delightfully cruel satire about Hollywood greed. Barbara Crampton (long may she reign!) plays a studio executive with the manic confidence of a coked-out Suze Orman, presiding over an ill-advised attempt to reproduce beloved characters via digital scans. The premise begins with some vaguely annoying commentary on the death of linear TV before plunging into a first-person chase sequence that reads like going through the haunted love tunnel of a deranged theme park. Screenwriter Zoe Cooper supplies a total of four would-be victims for Zhan to dispatch, and the puppets quickly pick off the first three in some amusing and inventive ways. It’s the fourth meat sack who isn’t so lucky, facing a dragged-out demise that’s not just uncomfortable to endure but oddly embarrassing to witness. From the recent theatrical horror hit “Buddy” to the surreal Showtime series “Kidding,” there are a staggering number of genre productions that have succeeded by turning cute clumps of felt into vehicles for something seriously fucked up. What sets “Dance, Dance, Dance, Dance” apart is its outstanding control over the inevitable, gaining its power through the brutal deliberateness of its torture.   The segment’s instantaneously irritating jingle offers an earworm you just don’t want in your head while you’re watching someone else lose theirs — but much like an unwanted playlist from a secret admirer, this bite-sized nightmare insists you engage with what Zhan has prepared for you, like it or not. The rest of “V/H/S Mixtape” is less nimble, and that leaves the outing mostly a wash. For his part, Moreau contributes “Heartbeat,” in which something like “The Descent” and something like “The Backrooms” perform a nonsensical duet of survival horror that’s been done better before. When a pair of urban explorers venture into an underground facility associated with sinister audio experiments, the segment’s vlogging setup gets caught between its familiar visual format and the installment’s overarching musical theme. The couple winds up describing being tortured by the silence of this bizarrely engineered cavern more than the film actually tries to make the audience experience it, and that’s disappointing coming from a director whose recent work suggested a more cunning command of sensory horror. “Heartbeat” still has a cool set, and actors Julie Clergerie and Elie Kaempfen boast some incredible chemistry. (Plus, a nasty little tattoo joke gives the whole ordeal some welcome bite if you’re paying close attention.) Dickerson’s “The Music of Mr. Sze” is infinitely more frustrating, as the esteemed cinematographer brings outsized visual sophistication to a boarding-house mystery centering a string musician and a young man wearing a pair of smart glasses. The second those two elements meet, it’s clear we’re cooked, and you can’t help but wonder what might have happened if someone else had written Dickerson’s “V/H/S” contribution. That said, there’s something about being held captive inside another person’s questionable taste that can really work for certain horror anthologies, and the director at least comes off wonderfully playful here. Finally, RZA’s “Death Tone” fares somewhat better than those two sections, even if it plays like the micro-budget baby of “High Fidelity” and “American Mary.” Neela Jolene stars as a young sound engineer grieving her recording-artist father while pursuing a legendary stage of her own. Unfortunately, her dad’s musical achievements relied on some profoundly perverse methods, and she’ll have to find her own way into the family business — critics be damned. Seemingly inspired by the dental-drill recording Billie Eilish famously sampled for “Bury a Friend,” “Death Tone” includes a fantastic sequence in which Jolene’s character remixes literal agony into an aggressively rhythmic track. The actress is an enormously entertaining presence, and the premise practically begs for an explosive music video finale. Instead, the ensuing spree sputters from one encounter to the next, leaving you with a choppy number that should go bigger and end sooner. As for a host, the shock-metal icons of GWAR appear throughout. That’s likely to inspire either affection or immediate exhaustion, depending on your fondness for the infamously disgusting performance group. A menagerie of rude and disgusting brutes, GWAR offers some objectively funny gross-out dialogue, but their “V/H/S Mixtape” segments are presented through such a cheap visual lens that it makes the band’s whole enterprise feel dated in a bad way. Having been around for more than four decades doing the same damn thing, GWAR continues to age into its accomplishments like a sweaty T-shirt. Generally, a great anthology wraparound should give the audience room to breathe — or gradually make the entire movie feel claustrophobic. The GWAR interludes try both and accomplish neither, while Forge’s contribution is astonishingly forgettable. Flying Lotus, conversely, offers a moonlit, monstrous animated interlude that’s beautiful and barely concerned with fitting the theme. In the end, it genuinely doesn’t have to be, although you do wonder why the filmmaker didn’t try something stranger after making movies like “Kuso.” Of course, that unevenness is all but encoded into the “V/H/S” DNA by this point. Originally conceived by Bloody Disgusting co-founder Brad Miska, the anthology series has survived a small carousel of distributors, an explosive streaming-era revival, and most recently, the addition of a new financial partner. None of that has erased the films’ core identity, and Zhan’s contribution to “V/H/S Mixtape,” in particular, serves as proof that the series can still introduce horror fans to earnestly exciting artists — while simultaneously educating them about pop culture frameworks they may have never personally experienced. But balancing those levels comes with a strange contradiction: Even as the “V/H/S” installments themselves remain fresh, the mat they fit feels progressively nostalgic. That’s an awkward position for a property whose modern reputation was made on cutting-edge discovery. Maybe, then, the solution is to stop insisting that “V/H/S” collections function as complete tapes. Troma Now, for example, has a randomizer built into its streaming catalog. It’s a single button that randomly takes you to any given nightmare the service has in stock: a brilliant idea that, sure, probably zero people reliably use… but imagine something similar for “V/H/S” segments! A short from 2012 might suddenly follow one from 2026, with no promise that the next selection would resemble either. If horror anthologies still make a decent case for the pleasures of manufactured randomness, actual randomness might be more exciting — and in that sense at least, “V/H/S Mixtape” has got the goods. So, do it: make the mixtape. Just don’t commit to a love letter. Shudder’s “V/H/S Mixtape” premieres on streaming October 9. title: Hanson v Faruqi: can the implied freedom protect racially harmful speech? - Law Society Journal
content: In Hanson v Faruqi [2026] FCAFC 96 (‘Hanson v Faruqi’), the Full Federal Court considered the meaning and application of sections 18C and 18D of the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth) (‘RD Act’), and the constitutional validity of those provisions, in the context of a (now infamous) tweet by Senator Hanson in response to a tweet by Senator Faruqi. This constitutes another contribution to recent and developing jurisprudence concerning the implied freedom of political communication. The primary judge had found Senator Hanson’s tweet breached section 18C and was not exempted under section 18D, and that the provisions were constitutionally valid. The Full Court held that none of the multiple grounds of appeal had been established and dismissed the appeal. In doing so, the Full Court did not agree with the primary judge on all matters. The Full Court considered the primary judge was wrong to proceed on the basis the provisions only slightly burdened political communication; instead finding the burden was significant. However, the Full Court declined to find the provisions’ adverse effects on the implied freedom were manifestly excessive, and therefore declined to find the provisions were not balanced. title: Honda CR-V Owners Tell a Car Buyer Who Commutes 14 Times A Week The Good And The Bad, Including 38 MPG - Torque News
content: The Honda CR-V is a popular crossover SUV, and one car shopper has it on their list. They’re looking for all-wheel drive, even though they arguably don’t need it, and something with excellent fuel economy, since they have a long commute about 14 times a week. It seems that they’re already leaning towards the CR-V, and they took some time to check the Internet to see what current CR-V owners have to say. “What are the good and bad of a Honda CR-V? I plan on getting a Honda CR-V this summer. I just wanna know the pros and cons of it. My current vehicle (Honda Pilot 2012) has some issues like it uses too much gas, it’s a 6 cylinder (I don’t need a 6, probably a 4). I live in NY so I’ll need a 4 wheel drive or all wheel drive for snow and bumpy roads where’s there’s construction (I drive everyday where the city does construction on the roads). And which CR-V should I get?” There were more than a few responses, and pretty much all were positive. Most suggested that this buyer might not need all-wheel drive, even living in New York City and driving to Long Island. Sure, it snows there, but it might not be so bad as to require AWD, and perhaps the CR-V can get by with front-wheel drive. Fuel economy also came up, with owners praising the hybrid for its ability to pass more gas pumps. “Hybrid. In cold climate the average MPG does fall some compared to Spring/Summer months. Just my own observations living in Canada. Otherwise, no issues,” one said. “Frankly, I think the CR-V, especially the hybrid top trim, is as good as it gets for a practical commuter vehicle in terms of efficiency aka price-performance ratio. All the amenities one needs in a car. All the safety suits and driver assists below still experimental self-driving. Great fuel economy. Perfectly ergonomic interior where everything makes sense. Cabin space. Outside looks. Reliability. It's got everything. Only downside I see is that when you're sitting in one, everything that you see inside is pretty much the same in top trim Civic and HR-V,” another said. As always, these comments are edited for grammar, content, and clarity. “2026 Sport Touring. Pros -great ride quality -great gas mileage (38mpg highway) -dead silent in the car -plenty of power in the hybrid -reliable. Cons (nitpicking) -Bose sound is a solid B+ and it took a lot of tuning to get it right -back up camera quality is pretty bad. I’m coming from a CX50, and that may have been the worst vehicle I’ve ever owned,” yet another said. “I just got a 2016 CR-V and it is fantastic. There is nothing I don't like about it. Which is weird because I'm super critical of cars. I drive my cars for years and years and never buy new. I also own a 2001 Accord that I love. Edit: We are running the Michelin Cross Climate tire this winter. Car came with ‘em already on. No problems in snow or ice so far,” another Reddit user said. We did see some cons, but reliability and the hybrid’s ability to come close to 40 MPG seemed to be on the minds of the majority of the respondents. That’s especially true with the hybrid. Very few comments didn’t mention the hybrid. Which makes sense given that the original poster apparently has a long commute 14 times a week, or essentially twice a day for seven day a week. That’s a lot of miles being piled up quickly, so a hybrid will help extend the amount of time being fillups. Pretty important always, but especially with fuel prices over $4 a gallon in much of the country these days. Have you had a positive experience owning a Honda CR-V? Or maybe a negative one? title: Men v. Food: Discovery Channel's New Series Features NFL Stars in Epic Food Challenges - Yahoo
content: One of food TV's most recognizable franchises is getting another helping. Man v. Food, the food reality series that originally debuted in 2008, is being reimagined as Men v. Food, an all-new Discovery Channel series set to premiere later this year. This time around, the show is adding a football twist. Former NFL stars Ryan Fitzpatrick and Vince Wilfork will co-host the new series, traveling to some of America's biggest football cities and facing off in massive food challenges. According to Discovery Channel, Fitzpatrick and Wilfork will visit a different NFL city each week in search of local favorites, hidden gems and larger-than-life dishes. They'll also team up with hometown legends before competing against each other in a game-day food showdown. Seattle, Kansas City, Boston and Buffalo are among the cities already confirmed, with additional locations still to be announced. "Few series have left a mark on pop culture quite like 'Man v. Food,' and we're excited to introduce a supersized new format that raises the stakes in every way," Joseph Boyle, Head of Content for Discovery Channel, said in a statement. Boyle added that Men v. Food will take what viewers loved about the original and give it "a fresh, competitive twist." "It's bigger, spicier, and has a whole new host of flavors," he said. Related: Food Network's Busiest Star Launches New Cooking Series Ahead of Another Highly Anticipated Show Premiere Man v. Food originally premiered on Travel Channel in December 2008 with Adam Richman as host. The premise was simple but memorable: Richman traveled around the country sampling a city's notable restaurants before attempting an enormous, spicy or otherwise daunting food challenge. Richman hosted the original run for four seasons, with the fourth retooled as Man v. Food Nation. The franchise was eventually revived in 2017 with Casey Webb taking over hosting duties. Webb continued hosting through the show's 10th season, which aired on Cooking Channel from September through November 2022. That makes Men v. Food the franchise's first new series in four years, although Discovery is changing much more than the title. Instead of one host taking on the food, Fitzpatrick and Wilfork will compete against each other. Both men spent years in the NFL: Fitzpatrick played quarterback for 17 seasons, while Wilfork is a two-time Super Bowl champion and former All-Pro defensive tackle. Discovery hasn't announced an exact premiere date for Men v. Food yet, but the series is expected to debut later in 2026. title: Seventh Circuit’s Franco v. Chobani Decision Confirms That FDA Enforcement Discretion Is No Shield Against Consumer Class Actions - JDSupra
content:
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit has revived a putative nationwide class action alleging that the food company Chobani deceptively marketed its Zero Sugar Greek yogurt, holding that the claims are not preempted by the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA). The July 27, 2026, decision is a pointed reminder that a federal agency’s decision not to enforce its own rules, even when reviewing labeling, does not neutralize exposure under state consumer protection statutes. For food, beverage and consumer product companies that have built labeling strategies around Food and Drug Administration (FDA) guidance rather than formal rulemaking, Franco v. Chobani materially recalibrates the risk calculus. Under FDA regulations, a product may not be labeled “sugar free” or “zero sugar” unless it contains less than 0.5 grams of sugars as defined in 21 C.F.R. § 101.9(c)(6)(ii), which in turn defines “Total Sugars” as “the sum of all free mono- and disaccharides (such as glucose, fructose, lactose, and sucrose).” Chobani’s yogurt was marketed as sugar-free but contained 4 grams of allulose per serving. Allulose is a naturally occurring monosaccharide not listed in FDA’s regulation. The plaintiffs sued under the consumer protection laws of numerous states, and because the FDCA expressly preempts state labeling requirements that conflict with federal standards, the case turned entirely on whether allulose is a “sugar” encompassed by FDA’s regulation that lists other types of sugars. In 2020, FDA issued guidance announcing its intent to exercise enforcement discretion for the exclusion of allulose from “Total Sugars” and “Added Sugars” declarations, “pending review of the issues in a rulemaking.” That rulemaking has never occurred. The district court nevertheless treated the guidance as controlling, deferred to it under Auer and dismissed on preemption grounds. Unlike Chevron deference, which has been permanently altered by Loper Bright (see below), Auer deference calls for courts to defer to an agency’s reasonable interpretation of its own regulations. The Seventh Circuit reversed. Invited to weigh in, FDA filed an amicus brief taking the position that § 101.9(c)(6)(ii) is unambiguous and captures all monosaccharides, including allulose. Although Chobani had received approval of its zero-sugar labeling from FDA, that approval was given under the agency’s enforcement discretion policy, not its regulation. The panel agreed, reasoning that the “such as” parenthetical is illustrative rather than limiting: “The FDA defined a class by way of chemistry; it reinforced that definition through examples, all of which share the same chemical structure.” In other words, because allulose is a monosaccharide, it is a sugar that counts toward “total sugars” under FDA’s regulation. Because the plaintiffs sought to enforce standards identical to the federal ones, their claims survived preemption. The court separately held that deception was plausibly alleged, rejecting Chobani’s argument that consumers care about sugar’s health effects rather than its chemistry (allulose is not absorbed by the body in the same way as other sugars): “Whether reasonable consumers care about the existence of allulose in their yogurt isn’t the same thing as asking whether reasonable consumers would be deceived by it.” Chobani did not merely rely on generalized guidance. It obtained a temporary marketing permit that required submission of its proposed label to FDA’s Office of Nutrition, Food Labeling and Critical Foods, which demanded revisions to the allulose- and sugar-content portions and then published its approval in the Federal Register. The court was unmoved: While Chobani may reasonably have believed it was safe from federal enforcement, “the agency’s marketing permit said nothing about state law consumer protection suits,” and Chobani was “a sophisticated actor” that should have known FDA’s enforcement priorities “would not immunize the company” from state law claims. This is the familiar cycle of regulatory ambiguity in acute form. Enforcement discretion paired with the slow pace of the rulemaking process opens space for a marketing claim that may be consistent with but technically outside the letter of the law; the promised rulemaking never arrives; and the plaintiffs’ bar converts the gap between the unamended regulation and the agency’s enforcement posture into a state law deception theory. The Seventh Circuit’s decision makes this flywheel even more harrowing for food, beverage and consumer products companies because draft guidance and enforcement discretion make up the vast majority of FDA’s regulation in the food space. It is unclear how this decision would have come out under Chevron. Under the previous regime, FDA may have received more deference to its scientific view that allulose, while a monosaccharide, should be treated differently when it comes to contributing to the total sugar content of foods. But, under Loper Bright, this interpretation is a judicial task. (See our July 9, 2024, client alert “Supreme Court’s Overruling of Chevron Deference to Administrative Agencies’ Interpretations of Statutes Will Invite More Challenges to Agency Decisions.”) The court adopted its position citing Loper Bright alongside Kisor, while acknowledging that an agency’s views may still be informative under Skidmore. The practical consequence is that courts will independently determine whether informal guidance carries the force of law without deferring to the agency’s scientific judgment or rationale in all cases. FDA’s assertion that its enforcement posture should govern also carries correspondingly less weight. Notably, Franco also illustrates that an agency’s litigating position can prevail over its own published guidance. Companies that structure labeling around guidance rather than rulemaking bear that exposure. Franco binds only federal courts in Illinois, Indiana and Wisconsin, and other courts may reach different conclusions on preemption, enforcement discretion and questions the panel left open — including “no added sugar” claims. Chobani also preserved additional arguments for remand, including a preemption theory based on FDA’s label approval and Monsanto Co. v. Durnell. Even so, the immediate lesson is durable: Federal regulatory comfort and state law litigation risk are separate inquiries, and white space creates litigation risk. title: The Hamilton (Democrat) v. Incumbent Marshall (Republican) in the Kansas U.S. Senate Race - Daily Kos
content:

			publication. The Super-”Red” Sunflower State of Kansas? –Will It Flip “Blue” and Oust Toxic Incumbent GOP Freshman Senator Roger Marshall for Democrat Adam Hamilton?   October 8, 2026 Kansas–the Sunflower State. The State was also labeled “Bleeding Kansas” in the 19th Century because violent skirmishes took place there in the lead-up to the Civil War.  Kansas, of course, is also  known for its terrible tornadoes, not only from the children’s “Wizard of Oz,” fictional tale, but also, in modern day life. In 2007, a 205- mile-per-hour twister destroyed the town of Greensburg. GOP leaders from President Dwight D. “Ike” Eisenhower and GOP Senate Leader Bob Dole grew up in Kansas as well. In addition to those Republican leaders, the Sunflower State was as politically “Red” as “Wizard of Oz’s”  heroine Dorothy’s “ruby red slippers.”  Although KS now has a popular Democratic Governor, 2nd- term Governor Laura Kelly, it has a 9D v. 31R State Senate and a 37D v. 87 R  State House. Its most current U.S. House line-up consists of 1D v. 3Rs. The last time a Democratic Presidential nominee won KS was in 1964 when in his landslide against Barry Goldwater, incumbent LBJ narrowly took that state. The last time KS elected a U.S. Democratic Senator was, get this, 94 years ago in 1932.https://thealmanacofamericanpolitics.com, 2026, National Journal, 2024, pp. 699-702 Well, in midterm Campaign 2026, Democrats and many political analysts believe that “Team Blue” has a fairly good chance to flip junior GOP U.S. Senator Roger Marshall’s seat  with its candidate Adam Hamilton. It’s time to look at this contest. El Dorado, Kansas native Roger Marshall (66) is currently serving his first term in the United States Senate and is running for re-election in the November 2026 midterms. Marshall graduated from KS State University with a B.S. in biochemistry. He received a medical degree from the University of Kansas. In 1998, after completing his residency as an OB/GYN, Marshall and eight other doctors opened Great Bend Regional Medical Center in Great Bend, KS where he practiced as an OB/GYN. He served in the U.S. Army Reserve for seven years, reaching the rank of captain. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Marshall In 2016, Marshall ran in the GOP primary for KS’s 1st U.S. Congressional District. After defeating the GOP incumbent Tim Huelskamp by 12 points in his primary, he ran unopposed by any Democrat in this “ultra-Red” district, and defeated the independent and Libertarian candidates with 65.9% of the vote.  During the primary, Huelskamp ran ads criticizing Marshall for confronting a neighbor over a 2008 land dispute. The neighbor had made a 911 call accusing Marshall of attempting to run him over with a car. Marshall pleaded no contest to a reckless driving misdemeanor and settled the neighbor’s civil suit. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Marshall In 2018, Marshall handily won his primary and re-election again. This time, in his re-election, he took 68.1% of the vote. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Marshall In October 2019, Marshall was one of 15-30 House GOPers led by firebrand GOP Rep. Matt Gaetz of FL who broke into a  confidential hearing of the House Intelligence Committee that was listening to testimony in connection with Donald’s first impeachment involving his shakedown of Ukraine. Marshall called the impeachment hearing a “sham.” https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Marshall In 2020, Marshall ran for the U.S. Senate. He beat the very controversial KS Sec. of State Kris Kobach in the primary and then went on to defeat his Democratic opponent by 9 points. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Marshall In the Senate, Marshall continued to have a far right record. He opposed abortion and called for the pro-choice “Roe v. Wade” decision to be overturned, which the Supreme Court did in 2022 and which Kansans later strongly voted to protect.  Marshall  used his background as a former MD to bolster his opposition to abortion. He was a 2020 election denier. Even after the January 6, 2021 deadly U.S. Capitol riot, he voted to object to the certification of Biden’s wins in AZ and PA. He also voted against creating an independent commission to investigate the 2021 Capitol attack. During the COVID-19 pandemic, he promoted conspiracy theories falsely suggesting that the Center for Disease Control was inflating the number of deaths involved. He was against face mask mandates and MD Marshall promoted the nonsensical use of hydroxychloroquine backed by Trump, and claimed that he had used it himself. He often went maskless at appearances during  this pandemic. He also rejected the scientific consensus on climate change, utter right-wing propaganda. He further supported repealing Obamacare, endorsed Trump’s top 1% tax cut, and Trump’s second term’s harsh tariffs policy. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Marshall Once again, you get the idea. Marshall’s 2026 midterm opponent Adam Hamilton (62) was raised in Prairie Village, KS. When he was a child, his parents divorced. Although he attended fundamentalist Oral Roberts University where he earned a 1985 degree in pastoral ministry, he went on to earn a degree in theology from more liberal Southern Methodist University and became a more liberal mainline pastor.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Hamilton_(pastor) Hamilton was the founding pastor of the United Methodist Church of the Resurrection in Leawood, Kansas. The church began in 1990 with just a few people who met in a small chapel at a local funeral home. It grew into the largest United Methodist Church congregation in the U.S. It has an average weekly attendance of about 25,000 across nine locations and has online television services. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Hamilton_(pastor) Hamilton preached at the National Prayer Service as part of the 2013 presidential inauguration festivities for Barack Obama’s second term. In 2016, Pres. Obama appointed Hamilton to the President’s Advisory Council on Faith-Based and Neighborhood Partnerships. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Hamilton_(pastor) Hamilton announced his candidacy for the U.S. Senate in KS in April 2026 and won the Democratic Senate primary to challenge GOPer Marshall. Politically, Hamilton describes himself as a centrist. He has stated that his congregation is a near mix of Democrats, Republicans, and independents. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Hamilton_(pastor) He can, therefore, work easily with people holding various viewpoints, which would serve him well in D.C. Can Hamilton upset Marshall in normally “Ruby-Red” Kansas?  Based on KS’ usual political history of rock-ribbed Republican voting, this race should have been out of reach for Democrats. Trump won here in 2024 by 16 points and also won in 2016 and 2020.  However, 2026, is not a “normal” midterm campaign year. Polls have called this race a “nail-biter,” and Hamilton could pull an upset. A newly released New York Times/Siena Poll of likely KS voters have Hamilton and Marshall tied at 45% each. https://www.kmbc.com/article/kansas-senate-race-poll-roger-marshall-adam-hamilton-tied/74040869  A recent Emerson College Poll (ECP) finds Hamilton leading Marshall 45%-43%, another extremely close result. The respected Cook Political Report calls this race a “Toss Up,” as does the website RealClearPolitics. Hamilton, however, has the strong disapproval of Trump even among Kansas voters going for him. title: Religious liberty, farming, & climate change coming to the Court - Pacific Legal Foundation
content: How was your summer? Sacramento is squeezing in its last gorgeous days of warm weather. The Supreme Court, meanwhile, has had enough of a vacation. Time to get back to work saving the Constitution! The October 2026 term began today with the first oral arguments. We also got three new grants out of the Court’s “long conference” on Friday: Missionaries of St. John v. Frederic, a religious liberty case that’s also about the right to build (so that’s fun!); Marschner v. Marschner, about disability benefits in a military divorce; and Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, an immigration case. Two PLF petitions were denied this morning: Thompson v. Wilson, a Fourth Amendment case brought by a Maine lobsterman, and Majestic Realty Co. v. Salazar, a First and Fifth Amendment case that asked the Court to revisit PruneYard. Alas. The Court’s calendar still has open seats—ideally for one or more of PLF’s 11 still-pending petitions—but even with what’s already on the docket, we have plenty to talk about. Note: This season, SCOTUS Scoop is trying a new format. The first scoop in our newsletter will always be a quick taste of what’s happening at the Court. The second lingers over a couple of cases. And the third gets the full sundae treatment. Let’s dig in. First case out of the gate — Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County: Boulder wants oil companies to pay for the alleged local costs of climate change, so it sued under state law over emissions produced around the world. The companies argue that federal law leaves no room for a state-law suit of that scope. An admirably immodest dispute to open the term. The hardest case to understand — Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota: Arizona’s rules on proof of citizenship for voting in state elections mean that it sometimes removes voters from the federal election rolls. The case has enough moving parts that I may need a whiteboard, three colors of marker, and a snack. The basic question: Who gets to set the rules for voter eligibility and maintaining voter registration rolls, and what happens when state procedural and federal substantive rules collide? The case with the best facts — Grand v. City of University Heights: Daniel Grand is an Orthodox Jew whose religion requires him to pray three times a day with a group of at least 10 men. Rather than walking back and forth to synagogues on the outskirts of town, strollers and kids in tow in the brutal Cleveland winters, he sought to host prayer gatherings in his home. A neighbor complained, and the city sent him a cease-and-desist letter, claiming these gatherings required a special use permit (even though a gathering of 10 to watch a Cleveland Browns game, for example, would’ve been just fine). Grand applied for a permit, but later withdrew after encountering local hostility. He then sued, but the city says he should have waited for a final decision on his permit application first. Apparently, in the city’s view, being told to stop praying at home is premature grounds for a lawsuit. Most likely to overturn longstanding precedent — Kian v. Florida: Since 1970, states have been allowed to convict people of serious crimes with six-person juries. The Sixth Amendment guarantees the right to a trial by “jury,” and dating back to common law, a “jury” was considered to mean 12 people. But more than five decades ago the Supreme Court decided that six could do just as good a job as a dozen. This term, the Court will decide whether that ruling should stand or whether the Constitution’s text should trump judges’ functionalist approach. Best sequel — Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards: The Labor Department ordered a New Jersey farm to pay back wages and penalties for alleged violations of a federal farmworker program. After SEC v. Jarkesy questioned the government’s habit of seeking monetary penalties before its own in-house adjudicators, the farm argues this dispute belongs in a real federal court, too. The Court will now decide whether the agency can keep the case in-house. Most consequential for religious liberty — St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy: Colorado pays for children to attend participating preschools but excludes Catholic schools when they use admissions policies requiring families to support Catholic beliefs about sex and gender. The state makes exceptions to its equal-access rule for other schools. Under Employment Division v. Smith, judges usually defer to generally applicable rules that don’t uniquely burden religion. The question here is when enough exceptions turn something “generally applicable” into something more selective that triggers heightened judicial scrutiny. The case doing the most cleanup — Viramontes v. Cook County: Cook County and Connecticut restrict possession of AR-15-style rifles. Gun owners say the rifles are commonly possessed for lawful purposes and therefore protected by the Second Amendment; the governments emphasize their dangerous characteristics and military parallels. How does a right written in the eighteenth century protect a rifle invented in the twentieth? And how do Heller’s “common use” rule and Bruen’s history test fit together? Originalism gets a practical exam. After a prison fight, Kekai Watanabe says he endured months of pain while requesting to see a doctor before learning his tailbone was fractured. He alleges that a prison nurse brushed off his request to go to a hospital, showing deliberate indifference to his medical needs in violation of the Eighth Amendment. You’d think that when you allege that a federal official violated your constitutional rights, you could sue for damages—even if Congress hasn’t explicitly said you can. But the truth is more complicated. In 1971, Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents recognized a damages suit against federal officers for a Fourth Amendment violation even without a statute expressly authorizing one. And in 1980, the Court allowed a suit against federal prison officials for deliberate indifference to medical needs in Carlson v. Green. But since then, the Court has become reluctant to recognize damages suits against federal officials unless they closely match one of the earlier cases, reasoning that the separation of powers requires it to leave remedies to Congress. Nielsen says this claim differs enough from Carlson that only Congress can authorize it; Watanabe says his claim falls squarely within that precedent. We’ll see whether the Court rules that the cases are similar enough, makes it harder for claims to fit within earlier precedent, or walks back Carlson and Bivens altogether. Ken Jouppi ran an air taxi to remote Alaskan villages. A passenger chartered his plane to Beaver, a village that prohibits alcohol, and brought beer aboard. Troopers stopped them before the plane left, and Jouppi was convicted of knowingly transporting alcohol. Alaska fined him, jailed him, and now it wants to seize his $95,000 airplane. Jouppi contends that would be an unconstitutional excessive fine. The question in Jouppi is how a court measures “excessive.” Alaska’s high court emphasized the general harms of bringing alcohol into dry villages and upheld the forfeiture even assuming Jouppi was culpable for only six beers. Jouppi argues that courts must look at what this defendant actually did, rather than the worst harms the category of offense might cause. My own view is that the Eighth Amendment protects an individual right, which requires looking at a person’s particular circumstances rather than resorting to generalities. The Supreme Court has filled only part of its new-term calendar. Here at PLF we’re hoping the justices add to their docket by taking one of the pending petitions we’ve filed, ranging from New York City lofts to continuing medical education. Here’s a sampler. For a time, SoHo was reserved for government-certified artists. That never worked out well, and now many residents who aren’t artists—or at least aren’t certified ones—live in lofts still subject to that old rule. The city now lets owners convert those lofts to ordinary residential use—but demands more than $100 per square foot to apply, saying it will give that money to an Arts Fund. We’re arguing that’s an exaction, and the question in this case is whether the constitutional limits on what governments may demand in exchange for land-use permits apply when the demand is money, rather than a slice of land. New York’s highest court said those limits did not apply to this fee. The distinction is awfully convenient for a government that prefers checks to easements. Maryland’s largest school district changed admission to its competitive magnet middle schools, including by considering whether applicants have enough high-achieving peers at their home schools and by norming the admissions test to the local school’s economic status. Asian American parents allege the changes were designed to reduce Asian American enrollment. The question in our petition is narrower, and important: If officials adopt facially neutral criteria for a discriminatory purpose, must the plaintiffs first show it reduced a group’s representation below the share of the applicant pool before a court will even consider evidence it was intended to disadvantage that group? Dr. Azadeh Khatibi is a licensed ophthalmologist who teaches continuing medical education courses on retinal tumors and other subjects. California, however, now requires continuing medical education courses to include discussion of implicit bias regardless of the course’s subject or whether the speaker disagrees. Dr. Khatibi and her co-plaintiff Do No Harm say the state is unconstitutionally dictating her speech. The Ninth Circuit treated the courses as government speech, meaning the government can shape them freely without any First Amendment implications. Our petition asks whether the state can avoid First Amendment scrutiny by recasting private speech in a regulated industry as the government’s own. I read a book about Florence Allen, the first woman to do so many things (including becoming the first woman judge) that “trailblazer” starts to sound like a modest job title. It got me thinking… what makes a “first” worth remembering? Read my review for The Dispatch here. I recently previewed the upcoming Supreme Court term for the Cato Institute’s Constitution Day. Catch the video here. I also wrote about some interesting dissents for SCOTUSblog, including Wong Kim Ark and birthright citizenship, Williams v. Florida and six-person juries, and NFL v. North American Soccer League and football v. soccer at the Supreme Court. I also won a case where a city had put a man in handcuffs for handing a homeless person a burrito. And of course, I watched a ton of U11 soccer. #ProudMom. Subscribe to the weekly Docket for dispatches from the front lines. title: Report: Honda Delays Next-Gen CR-V Production to April 2027 - Yahoo Autos
content: Honda is reportedly delaying the launch of the next-generation, hybrid-only CR-V. The reason is a good problem to have - dealers can't stop selling the current one, with cars lasting all of two weeks on dealer lots before finding new homes, a turn rate almost unheard of. According to Automotive News, Honda wants to squeeze out as many 2027 models as physically possible before shutting down to retool the factory. The CR-V is Honda's workhorse in North America - it's responsible for nearly 10 percent of the brand's total sales in America. Dealer inventory is hovering at a lean 17-day supply, so Honda has reportedly made the extraordinary decision to push back the start of production for the redesigned 2028 CR-V by three months to April 2027. "Honda has not announced any information on future CR-V model changes," was the response AutoGuide received from Honda rep Chris Naughton. "We cannot comment on speculation about launch." The report's math claims that holding back the redesigned CR-V by a few months will dent the new crossover's first-year production output by a projected 6.7 percent. But it also sounds like Honda isn't really bothered by that shortfall on the front end, with the automaker now reportedly changing its original plan to keep building the Civic at its Greensburg, Indiana plant. Instead, the Indiana facility-which currently builds both the CR-V and Civic hatchback-will become a dedicated CR-V sanctuary. Moving the Civic out of Indiana should allow for at least an additional 70,000 CR-Vs. That means the next-generation Civic sedans for all of North America will roll out of Honda's plant in Alliston, Ontario, Canada. Meanwhile, the five-door Civic hatchback will be imported from Japan once the shuffle takes effect. It begs the question: is Honda betting on import tariffs ending sooner rather than later? title: NFL today: How to watch Buccaneers v Cowboys, TV channels & live stream Thursday 8 October - The Guardian
content: How will the Buccaneers and Cowboys fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options The bad news for the Buccaneers: Their 0-4 start has been an unmitigated disaster that, in normal circumstances, would have already evaporated their playoff chances. The good news for Tampa Bay, however, is that they play in the NFC South, meaning they’re still just two games out of a tie for the lead in what is often the worst division in the NFL. All is not quite lost yet. If the Bucs want to join the 1992 Chargers and become the second team to make the postseason after an 0-4 opening, they’ll need to stop the bleeding on Thursday night in north Texas. They’ll have to do it without Baker Mayfield, who continues to nurse an injury to his throwing thumb. They’ll face a challenge against the Cowboys, who are just 2-2 but look like slim favorites in the NFC East while the Eagles struggle to get out of neutral. The Cowboys have gotten an excellent first four games from Dak Prescott, who has paced one of the most efficient offenses in football. No team is scoring more than Dallas’ 3.4 points per offensive series, and it’s been Prescott and the passing game doing most of that work. (Nearly 75%t of Dallas’ yards have come through the air, compared to a league average of two-thirds.) A big outing against Tampa Bay would solidify the Cowboys’ path to a division title. United Kingdom: Watch on Sky Sports NFL or Sky Sports Main Event, or stream with NOW or NFL Game Pass on DAZN. Jerry Jones loves a splashy deal, and he made one before last week’s win over the Texans. The Cowboys sent out a package built around a second-round draft choice to bring in Steelers cornerback Joey Porter, who didn’t make a Pro Bowl in his first four seasons but established himself as one of the league’s tougher man-to-man cover players all the same. The next touchdown Porter surrenders as the primary defender on a target will be the first of his career. Dallas made the deal without giving Porter the new contract that had eluded him in Pittsburgh, suggesting Jones saw his acquisition as a win-now endeavor. The Bucs will ride for another week, at least, with rookie QB Jalon Daniels. The Kansas product made his debut in Week 4 and finished 27th of the league’s 32 QBs in passer rating that week, and dead last in yardage per attempt. He sprinkled in a pair of interceptions — not an ideal start for a rookie who is about to turn 24 and whose six years of collegiate experience might have suggested a less rocky debut. Will Daniels find it hospitable to go up against the team that is dead-last in the NFL in net yards allowed per passing attempt (8) through the first four weeks? Tampa Bay’s last flickers of hope depend on it.

title: Honda Axes Plan For Civic Production In Indiana And Pushes Back Next-Gen CR-V - Carscoops
content:
Honda's next-generation CR-V and Civic models will use a lighter architecture and more advanced hybrid powertrain In an effort to boost profits, Honda is reportedly planning a major shake-up of its U.S. production plans for the next-generation CR-V and the future Civic sedan. While this will mean shoppers will have to wait longer to get behind the wheel of the new CR-V, they will have more time to pick up the keys to an outgoing model. The next-generation CR-V, which has yet to be revealed, is expected to premiere before the end of this year, or in early 2027. It will introduce an improved hybrid powertrain that’ll cost less to produce and be more efficient. Production had initially been penciled in to start around January, but reports say it has been delayed until April 2027. Read: Honda’s Next-Gen Hybrids Will Arrive Next Year, Starting With The CR-V Production of the new model is tipped to first begin at the carmaker’s Alliston, Ontario, Canada, facility before U.S. manufacturing starts. Auto News also states that Honda now plans to build 41,315 units in North America during the first year of production, dropping its monthly output by 6.7%. It’s unclear why exactly Honda is delaying the new CR-V by several months, but it’s probably because of how popular the current version is. Through the first nine months of this year, CR-V sales are up 9.5% to 336,844 units. It was especially popular in September with 34,788 sold, a 17% increase from September of last year. This easily makes it Honda’s best-selling model with almost twice as many sold as the Civic in second place, which shifted 17,724 units last month. As the current CR-V is now four years old, these figures are impressive. The CR-V isn’t the only model that Honda is tweaking production plans for. It had planned to build the next-generation Civic at its site in Greensburg, Indiana, in May 2028, but unnamed supply chain sources claim these plans have been scrapped. In response to these claims, Honda told CarScoops that, “Regarding Civic, that information was not released by Honda, and we don’t speculate on future production plans.” The carmaker added, “We have not confirmed any launch timing for CR-V.  With the current CR-V at about 17-day supply, setting sales records, and our customers and dealers demanding more supply, we of course continue to build that vehicle.” This has likely been done to free up capacity at the Indiana plant, which will also build the new CR-V. Given that the CR-V is selling in far greater numbers than the Civic, and is more profitable, it’s logical for Honda to want to build more of them on local shores. While the next-gen Civic will no longer be manufactured at the Indiana site, the current plan is still for the new Civic sedan to be built at the Ontario plant, starting in April 2028. In scrapping production of the Civic hatchback in Indiana, Honda will be forced to start importing this model from Japan. The new Honda CR-V and Civic will shift to the company’s next-gen mid-size platform that shaves off 198 lbs (90 kg) over equivalent current models. In addition, hybrid versions will use a new direct-injection 2.0-liter inline-four with new electric motors and the same S+ Shift simulated gears as the Prelude. title: Larry V. Laugen - Fillmore County Journal
content: October 8, 2026 by Fillmore County Journal Leave a Comment Larry V. Laugen was born to Edwin C. and Clara J. Laugen (Foss) on September 4, 1935, in La Crosse, Wisconsin. He grew up in Harmony, Minnesota, and graduated from Harmony High School in 1953. After a semester at Luther College, he enlisted in the U.S. Army. He spent two of his three years in the army, serving in Germany. After release from active duty, he returned to Luther College. He transferred to Winona State University and graduated from there in 1960. In 1958, he met the love of his life, Eloise Jetson, at the Avalon Ballroom in La Crosse. They would continue their love of dancing to big band music for their whole life. Eloise and Larry were married in Spring Grove, Minnesota, on January 3, 1959. On January 5, 1960, a son, Steve, was born. After graduation from Winona State in the summer of 1960, Larry worked for Federated Insurance as a claims adjuster and underwriter. During that time, a daughter, Julie, was born on December 31, 1961. In 1964, Larry was hired by IBM Rochester. Over the next 29 years with IBM, he worked on different projects in Rochester, Minnesota (1964-70, 1975-78); Boulder, Colorado (1970-72, 1978-93); Fort Worth, Texas; and Gaithersburg, Maryland. After retirement from IBM, Larry and Eloise moved to Loveland, Colorado. They were busy volunteering as Stephen Ministers for their church, and for the sculpture shows in Loveland. In addition, Larry enjoyed playing golf, flying and spending winters on South Padre Island, Texas. It has been a good and interesting life, enriched by the love of Eloise, Steve (Jeanette), Julie, grandchildren, great-grandchildren, and friends. He was predeceased by his parents Edwin and Clara Laugen, and son-in-law Steve Green. He is survived by his wife Eloise, son Steve (Jeanette), daughter Julie, five grandchildren and five great-grandchildren. title: Suncor v. Boulder Oral Arguments: Early Signals from the Justices - Independence Institute
content: Did you know we have a news site? At Complete Colorado, we aggregate the most important news from around Colorado and also feature original reporting. Our investigative journalists bring you stories the mainstream media won’t cover. From Grand Junction to Limon, Complete Colorado has you covered. Check us out! On October 5, eight Justices of the U.S. Supreme Court heard oral arguments in Suncor Energy (U.S.A.) Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County (Suncor v. Boulder County). The case asks whether state and local governments can impose liability on American companies for emitting carbon dioxide and affecting global climate. Dozens of other jurisdictions have filed similar suits in state courts. Justice Samuel Alito recused himself from the case a mere week before it was argued. Although the reason was not disclosed until after the arguments, he explained that he and his wife own individual stock in oil companies (ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66, neither of which is named in Suncor). If the Justices split 4-4, the case could be allowed to proceed to trial and a jury in a single U.S. county could hold companies liable for a global product. After nearly two hours of oral arguments on Monday, the eight remaining Justices sent “mixed signals” on whether climate cases should be allowed to proceed in state courts. Boulder County argues that the lawsuit isn’t attempting to regulate greenhouse gas emissions. Rather, the production and marketing of fossil fuels by Suncor and ExxonMobil, while knowing and misrepresenting the risks, have caused or contributed to harms in Colorado, and the county seeks compensation for these harms — so the argument goes. Several Justices sounded skeptical. “Is there anything anomalous in your mind to applying state law here to worldwide conduct?” Justice Neil Gorsuch asked. “No, I don’t think so,” Mr. [Kevin] Russell [attorney for Boulder] replied, comparing Boulder’s claims to a product liability lawsuit against an auto maker for a defective car. This is an odd analogy since the county isn’t arguing that oil is defective. Far from it. Oil is vital to the economy and everyday living, and Boulder County hasn’t sought to ban it. Product liability suits also require plaintiffs to show they have suffered direct harm as a result of a particular defendant’s products. Boulder hasn’t done so. The energy companies advance the argument that one state can’t regulate inherently interstate matters and that federal law has traditionally had oversight over interstate air and water pollution. Their lawyer, Kannon Shanmugam, described Boulder’s claims as an “unprecedented effort to use state law to regulate global conduct.” Justice Elena Kagan seemed skeptical of that, arguing that the approach “appears to be based on the old 1990s tobacco suits” which had been allowed to proceed. But even Justice Kagan pointed out that “everything depends on this idea that the defendants are responsible for excessive emissions.” Chief Justice John Roberts agreed, and Justice Brett Kavanaugh said the Court’s precedents make it “crystal clear” that issues involving interstate air and water pollution are subject to federal preemption. The lawyer for Boulder County admitted to Justice Clarence Thomas that under their arguments, there would be nothing stopping suits against large retailers; that could extend to gasoline, petrochemical manufacturers, and even dairy farmers, since cows emit methane. Roberts noted the “practical matter” of how it would work on the ground to manage a slew of 50 or so similar or identical lawsuits following on the heels of Suncor. The Independence Institute joined two amicus briefs urging the court to take the case and again on the merits, arguing that one state cannot make national energy policy, and companies cannot be beholden to hundreds or even thousands of separate environmental agencies. A ruling is due before the term ends next summer. If the Court ties, Colorado’s decision stands and the cases stayed in other states can resume.  Boulder’s attorney told Justice Amy Coney Barrett that the suit would make the companies “internalize a portion of the cost of their activities.” That cost will ultimately land not just on Colorado consumers, but national and international customers. title: Is Fury v Joshua about meritocratic sporting excellence or just algorithmic celebrity power? | Jonathan Liew - The Guardian
content: This long-awaited fight is happening exactly as intended: at the sweet spot where commercial potential meets a genuine absence of jeopardy The 1912 Olympic marathon was held in a brutal Scandinavian heatwave, and before long Shizo Kanakuri of Japan was flagging. His journey to Stockholm had been debilitating; he had barely trained and struggled to sleep. At around the 16-mile mark he finally gave in. Exhausted and disoriented, he stumbled off the road and into a garden party, where – according to his bemused hosts – he sat and drank orange juice for an hour. The next day, deeply ashamed at his failure to complete the race, he quietly took a boat back to Japan. In Sweden the mystery of the “disappearing runner” took on almost mythical proportions. Kanakuri’s name was on the country’s missing persons list for more than 50 years. In the 1960s, a journalist tracked him down to Kumamoto in southern Japan, where he worked as a geography teacher. At great expense, Swedish television flew him back to Stockholm and ferried him to the spot where he had abandoned the race. So it was that in March 1967, Kanakuri finally completed the 1912 Olympic marathon in a time of 54 years, eight months, six days, five hours, 32 minutes and 20.3 seconds. None of this, of course, was of the least sporting consequence. But it was a nice story, generating substantial interest, and the newspapers could fill their column inches, and the broadcasters could fill their schedules, and perhaps ultimately this was all that mattered. All of which brings us, by a similarly circuitous route, to Tyson Fury v Anthony Joshua, a heavyweight fight that is often wrongly described as happening several years too late, long after the 38-year-old Fury and the 36-year-old Joshua have passed their fighting peak, years since either man has beaten anyone of world-class pedigree, a delay that makes Mayweather v Pacquiao look impromptu. In fact Fury v Joshua is happening exactly as intended: at the sweet spot where commercial potential meets an absence of genuine jeopardy. Make this fight in 2021 and both men are putting titles, the undisputed crown, an entire fighting legacy, at terminal risk. Make it in 2031 and not even the combined bullshit wattage of Frank Warren, Eddie Hearn, Dana White and Turki al-Sheikh could persuade the public that this was anything other than a fairground sideshow. No: it has to be now, before anyone stops caring. Like a market trader extracting maximum price for a fruit on the very brink of going rotten, this is the fight business operating on God-tier mode. “We will get it on at the right time,” Joshua once said. That was in April 2016, when a fight with Fury would have been worth a fraction of the £150m it is worth now. When it comes to boxing, absence makes the purse grow fatter. That this is often regarded as a minor annoyance, a glitch in the system rather than a fundamental existential-level malfunction, is just one of the reasons for boxing’s slow drift towards mainstream irrelevance. Virtually every other sport on earth operates along the principle that at some point the best will meet the best, and assembles structures and rules and governing bodies that compel this into being. Boxing is pretty much the only sport in the world where this is not true, which raises the germane question of whether it can really be considered a sport at all, at least in the modern, codified sense. Naturally Fury has spent the past few weeks (Months? Years?) desperately trying to pin the blame on Joshua for not getting the fight made. In Fury’s tale of the tape, he has been ready and waiting this whole time. With the exception of the two and a half years he spent out of the sport dealing with a combination of doping charges, substance abuse, and mental health crises. Or the subsequent two and a half years he spent battling Deontay Wilder, not just in the ring but in the courts. As frequently thrilling as that trilogy of fights was, even at the time there was a sense we were missing out on something even greater; that as one rivalry was playing itself out, there were others suffering as a result. Then there were the retirements: around five in total, depending on how you count these things. It feels pleasingly nostalgic now to recall that Fury first quit boxing in 2013 (“1000000%, no matter what, ill never fight again”), then again in 2016, again in 2017 (“THE END”), again in 2022 (“the truth, the gospel truth, nothing but the truth, I’m done, no amount of material assets or money will make me come back”), and most recently from 2025 to 2026. I’m no expert in contract negotiation. But if you’re trying to establish yourself as a bona fide sporting and business partner, maybe stop retiring every few years? Cowardice will always be too strong a word for anyone who steps between those ropes and risks their health for our titillation. But it is a shame that a fight that could have defined an entire generation of British boxing is happening only when the stakes are so low. For all the biblical hype that will doubtless accumulate under the wheels over the next two months, what does this fight actually tell us? What gets settled or rewritten? Is it actually in anybody’s interests for anything to be settled or rewritten, given the potential for an even more lucrative rematch sometime in late 2027? Prizefighting owes its success to the ability to hold two ideas in its orbit at once. First, the sense of sporting ultimacy, the idea that what we are watching is a kind of pinnacle of raw human endurance, the very best fighting men and women on the planet. And second, the sense of vaudeville and pantomime, the deliberate and often provocative packaging of a product for entertainment and consumption. Boxing has always been at its greatest when each has been in the service of the other. A Christmas cracker requires the colourful wrapping and the bit that bangs in the middle. Remove either and the whole concept falls apart. But for years now, these ideas have been breaking in opposite directions. What we essentially have now is a sport increasingly rearranging around the two disparate poles of meritocratic sporting excellence and algorithmic celebrity power. In the former, Moses Itauma is one of this country’s best-kept sporting secrets, and an all-British world title clash between Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley is feted as one of the greatest fights of the decade but generates virtually zero wider recognition. In the latter, the internet pest Jake Paul is one of the sport’s most bankable names, the greatest heavyweight of his generation, Oleksandr Usyk, is fighting a kickboxer, Floyd Mayweather Jr is in talks about coming out of retirement to fight Mike Tyson, and Conor Benn and Chris Eubank Jr keep rematching for the next 10 years. Which world does Fury v Joshua belong to? Which half of the marathon are we being invited to watch? I want to believe – and so do Netflix – that Fury can still be the force of old, rather than an increasingly monotonous provocateur. I want to believe in the Joshua of the 2010s, unscarred and optimistic, this beautiful man of beautiful clean lines. I want to believe this is sport. But deep down, I think we all know the answer.
