title: Next-Gen Honda CR-V Could Be Delayed For The Best Possible Reason - CarBuzz
content: Subscribe to the CarBuzz newsletter to never miss an update We've updated this article with an official statement from Honda regarding CR-V and Civic production. Hondas are hot this year. The company's sales are up by nearly 5% over last year, and it had its best third-quarter sales since 2019. Arguably its biggest success this year has been the CR-V. It's up by nearly 10% this year, and it's almost guaranteed to become America's bestselling vehicle other than the whole Ford F-Series line. Some of that is due to the CR-V staying popular, but also because Toyota fumbled the new RAV4's launch. Honda also seems keen to ensure it doesn't lose any ground, as Automotive News reports the company is delaying production of the next-generation model. Automotive News spoke to an anonymous source who said that the production of the next CR-V has been pushed back three months to April of next year. The outlet didn't specify whether that delay is overall, or just for specific plants. Honda builds CR-Vs both at its factory in Indiana, and at one in Ontario, Canada. According to a previous report, production was expected to start first in Canada around February, followed by the Indiana plant a few months later. The April start date would seem to suggest the delay affects the Canada plant, but also that US production may come online even later. Either way, it's not a massive delay. The new model will likely still hit dealer lots well before the end of 2027. It might not even affect when Honda shows the world the new CR-V, which we still think could happen by the end of this year. Automotive News also reported that Honda has changed production plans for the next-generation Honda Civic sedan. It was supposed to be added to the Indiana production line alongside the hatchback, but apparently that plan has been scrapped. The current sedan is built on another line at the Ontario plant. CarBuzz contacted Honda seeking more information regarding CR-V and Civic production. A company spokesperson provided the following statement: "Honda has not announced any information on future CR-V model changes, so we cannot comment on speculation about launch timing. We are pleased to continue production of the current 2027 CR-V to meet strong customer demand and help replenish dealer inventories. Dealer inventory currently stands at approximately a 17-day supply, well below our ideal level. Regarding Civic, that information was not released by Honda and we don’t speculate on future production plans." The main reason that we can see for Honda delaying the next CR-V is because the model is so hot right now. Inventory levels are low right now, as noted by Automotive News. That, along with fantastic sales, is a great sign as far as demand goes, but only for as long as Honda can meet it. All of this demand is also for the current generation, and as long as demand is high for that, Honda likely doesn't want to risk missing out on some strong months of current-generation sales to switch over to the new one. We also wouldn't be surprised if Honda wants to be extra sure that it can start production of the new model smoothly. Toyota struggled to get production of the latest RAV4 up to speed this year. That snag effectively gave the sales crown to Honda. Other small SUVs have also been selling well this year, something that Toyota should've been able to capitalize on if it could've sent new RAV4s to lots. Furthermore, the Civic production change could also be related to the CR-V. As we've mentioned, Honda builds both the Civic hatchback and CR-V in Indiana. It would make sense for Honda to skip adding another body style to the Indiana factory in order to focus on CR-V production, either to make sure it continues to run smoothly, or even to add CR-V production volume. For reference, Honda has seen a bigger increase in both volume and percentage of the CR-V than the Civic this year. Besides the fact that it will probably be revealed in the next few months, we know that the next-generation model will be a big change. Honda has developed an entirely new platform, which will also show up in future Civic and Accord generations, that promises significant weight savings and improved refinement. It will still offer a four-cylinder hybrid powertrain, but it will be more efficient thanks to direct fuel injection and new motors. Toyota handed Honda an amazing opportunity, and Honda seems to know it. It seems to us that it's making sure it makes the most of the popularity of the current generation, and is buying time to make sure it can get the next one out with no issues. Toyota does seem to be getting RAV4 production and sales back on track, but Honda is surely going to do everything it can to stay a step ahead of its rival. title: L.Z. and D.Z. v. Italy - ECHR
content: Severed family ties between mother and child highlight systemic flaws in juvenile-justice and foster-care systems in Italy. In the case of L.Z. and D.Z. v. Italy, the Court held that there had been a violation of the right to respect for family life. The case concerned the severance of the relationship between a biological mother and her child, who had been abandoned on a pavement at birth by his father. Although the mother had taken steps to have the child returned to her, the Italian authorities had declared him abandoned and available for adoption and had then placed him in foster care in accordance with the expedited procedure. Subsequent court orders for the reunification of the mother and child had not been enforced. To date, the child has not been returned to his biological mother and decisions regarding contact arrangements have not been complied with. The Court noted that the domestic courts had failed to take prompt, practical and appropriate measures to establish effective contact between the first applicant and the child. Then, for some five years, they had “tolerated” the lack of contact between the applicants and the non-enforcement of the decision ordering their reunification. The passage of time had in fact become the key factor in support of keeping the child in the foster family rather than returning him to his mother. That factor had given rise to a fait accompli: the severance of family ties between the first applicant and her child. We don't know what your privacy preferences are yet.

title: Canon C50 or R6 V: Which One Fits the Way You Work? - Fstoppers
content: Canon now sells two compact full frame video cameras built around the same 32.5-megapixel 7K sensor, and $1,200 to $1,400 separates them, depending on whether the C50 is on sale. When the image coming off that sensor is nearly identical, your decision rests on heat, audio, stabilization, and how each camera behaves on an actual job. Both bodies shoot 3:2 open gate, record raw internally, and deliver oversampled 4K up to 60 fps along with 4K at 120 fps. Josh Sattin puts the Canon EOS C50 and Canon EOS R6 V side by side with the same lens and the same settings, and the Canon Log 2 footage is close enough that a grade built for one carries over to the other with only small differences. The one fix he makes is white balance, since the daylight preset sits around 5,200 K on the R6 V and 5,600 K on the C50. If you plan to run them as A and B cameras, mismatched presets will throw off a quick match long before the sensors do. Dynamic range is where a gap shows up. In a window test exposed for the highlights, then pushed hard in the shadows and viewed at 200%, the C50 holds slightly more shadow detail, in raw and in the compressed codecs alike. The margin is small, and you'll only see it when you're pulling detail out of a deliberately dark frame. High ISO behavior is closer than the spec sheets suggest. The C50 officially has dual base ISOs of 800 and 6,400 in Canon Log 2 and raw, while Canon doesn't list a second base ISO for any of its mirrorless bodies. Sattin's lens cap test, shot in raw and brightened to reveal the noise pattern, shows the R6 V cleaning up at the jump from ISO 5,000 to 6,400, just like the C50. Audio splits the two more clearly. The C50 ships with a top handle carrying XLR inputs, simple level controls, a record button, a lock, a zoom rocker, a cold shoe, a switchable tally light, and extra mounting points, and it locks firmly to the body without a cage. On the R6 V, you'd add the Tascam CA-XLR2d-C, which passes audio through the hot shoe and sounds great, though Sattin finds its single shoe mount less sturdy than the C50's handle. Canon has steadily added bodies without a viewfinder, from the EOS R50 V to these two, and the EOS R6 Mark III sits alongside them with a 32.5-megapixel sensor plus the EVF and mechanical shutter that stills shooters expect. Sony went down a similar road with the FX3, and Nikon followed with the ZR, each dropping the viewfinder in favor of a body shaped for rigs, gimbals, and monitors. Once the sensor stops being the deciding factor, you're really choosing an operating system, a cooling design, and an accessory ecosystem. The ISO result also points to a test you can run on any camera you own. Shoot a lens cap frame at each ISO step in raw, lift the exposure in post, and look for the step where the noise suddenly drops. Manufacturers don't always publish a second base ISO on hybrid bodies, and finding it yourself can show you that ISO 6,400 is a cleaner setting than 5,000 in a dim venue. Heat is the other clear divide. Canon publishes recording limits in its specifications, and Sattin has found those figures accurate across years of his own testing. Rated at 73 degrees Fahrenheit, the R6 V can record raw at 60 fps and oversampled 4K at 60 fps for 120 minutes or longer, while oversampled 4K at 30 fps, 4K at 120 fps, and the non-oversampled modes carry no stated limit. Any mode with a listed limit will shrink in summer heat and humidity, which Sattin deals with much of the year in North Carolina. He expects oversampled 4K at 24 and 30 fps to stay safe, so the risk concentrates on higher frame rates and raw outdoors. The C50's thicker body houses a more serious cooling system, and none of Canon's cinema cameras have shut down on him, even in punishing conditions. Sattin's take on stabilization, timecode, and more is in the video above. Alex Cooke is a Cleveland-based photographer and meteorologist. He teaches music and enjoys time with horses and his rescue dogs.

title: Nebraska tight end named semifinalist for William V. Campbell Trophy - Cornhuskers Wire
content: A starter on Nebraska’s offense is now a semifinalist for college football’s premier scholar-athlete award. Tight end Luke Lindenmeyer was named a semifinalist for the 2026 William V. Campbell Trophy. The Campbell Trophy recognizes an individual as the best football scholar-athlete in the nation for his combined academic success, football performance and exemplary leadership. Only seniors, graduate students, or graduate transfers who maintain a 3.2 GPA or higher and are participating in the 2026 season are eligible. Candidates must also have outstanding football ability as a first-team player or significant contributor and have demonstrated strong leadership and citizenship. Lindenmeyer is one of the 206 candidates from the FBS and FCS levels, as schools can nominate one student-athlete annually. He is in his fifth season with the Huskers and has made 44 appearances, including 25 starts. This season, Lindenmeyer has 12 catches for 116 yards and one touchdown. The tight end has also helped the team with his blocking. Nebraska ranks 17th nationally in rushing offense and 24th in the nation in total offense through five games. Off the field, Lindenmeyer has been active in Nebraska’s Life Skills program and is a four-time Tom Osborne Citizenship Team recipient. He was one of 27 student-athletes across all of Nebraska’s athletic programs to receive the Sam Foltz 27 Hero Leadership Award in 2024. He is also a three-time academic All-Big Ten pick and 2026 Big Ten Distinguished Scholar. The National Football Foundation (NFF) will announce 12-16 finalists on Oct. 21. The Campbell Trophy winner will then be announced in Las Vegas on Dec. 8. title: Liverpool v Manchester City: Andoni Iraola Provides Injury Update & Match Preview - Yahoo Sports
content: This Sunday, Liverpool face Manchester City at Anfield in both sides' first game after the international break. The match comes against the backdrop of the Premier League's Manchester City verdict, promising a raucous atmosphere at Anfield this weekend. Speaking ahead of the heavyweight clash, Andoni Iraola has provided an update on Liverpool's injury situation and reflected on his start to life at Liverpool. Most Liverpool fans would agree that Andoni Iraola has made a very positive impression during his first months at the club. It is not all about impressions, however; the Basque has also led Liverpool to an unbeaten start this season. The Reds have played seven matches so far, winning four and drawing three. Iraola spoke to beIN SPORTS ahead of his press conference on Friday: "I think the international break is a moment to reflect, because we normally have a crazier schedule. You go two, three days preparing the next game. Then you need, I think, a break, [to] analyse how the season has gone so far. I think we have a good amount of games already to analyse and see the things that we've done well and the things that I think can improve." Despite beginning the season unbeaten, Iraola still desires improvement. Talking about the club's targets this season, he said: "We don't have a specific points total or position, no. I think we have to arrive as high as we can, we have to be the best team we can be." "...If we can give these players a good platform, a good structure, we will be there fighting for titles, yes." Iraola discussed whether Alexander Isak or Cody Gakpo will be available to play against Manchester City. Both players were having superb starts to their respective international breaks before having to withdraw due to injury. Isak put away a clinical finish against Romania to open the scoring, whilst Cody Gakpo scored a last-minute volley to claw back a draw for the Netherlands against Jurgen Klopp's Germany. "It's a matter of if they are going to recover in time to help us in the next game or not. But right now they are both injured." This weekend's Anfield battle will be Iraola's first against Manchester City as Liverpool head coach and is likely to represent his biggest test so far. "We've [also] been unbeaten, but they've won all of them, so it makes a big difference in their side. I think we need to be very, very good if we want to beat City because they've been scoring a lot of goals lately. We know the names that are very dangerous. But I think also we've shown good defensive improvements lately, and I hope we can defend the threats that they have but also hurt them on the other side." "...It's a big game...I think we are playing against the team that is right now at the top of the league, so definitely it's an important game for us. We know we will have to be at our best, and also I know that the people [at Anfield] will be looking to help the team." On the pitch, Iraola has overseen Liverpool's transformation into a much more solid, much more compact side. This has been a huge improvement compared to last season. Whilst some doubts have arisen over the scarcity of wins compared to draws, going unbeaten is an achievement in itself that sets a foundation for the rest of the season. Even more impressive, however, has been Iraola's adaptation to Liverpool off the pitch. Much has been said about how he has looked to immerse himself in the club and city; his attendance at Liverpool Women's derby match against Everton earlier in the international break highlights this. He has taken to Liverpool undoubtedly well, and has been a strong character and personality fit for the club. That is why so many will be desperate to see a rip-roaring Liverpool performance at Anfield that leaves everything on the pitch - something that gives Iraola his first big, uniting moment. At issue is whether the administration can lawfully strip Harvard of federal funding and its ability to enroll international students. By 

                    Josh Moody Harvard, led by President Alan Garber (right), is facing several lawsuits from the Trump administration, which has sought to cut billions in federal funding from the university. Photo illustration by Justin Morrison/Inside Higher Ed | Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images | APCortizasJr/iStock/Getty Images | Joseph Prezioso/AFP/Getty Images Harvard University’s sprawling legal battle with the federal government is still grinding on. The private Massachusetts university and the Trump administration met twice in federal appeals court this week as Harvard attempted to repel efforts to cut off billions in research funding and restrict international enrollment. While Harvard picked up wins in the lower courts last year, the Trump administration appealed those rulings. On Monday, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit heard arguments in Harvard’s case against the Department of Health and Human Services and other federal agencies over their attempt to cancel more than $2 billion in federal research funding last year for allegedly failing to address antisemitism on campus. U.S. District Judge Allison Burroughs ruled last year that the cuts were unlawful and that the federal government violated the university’s First Amendment rights in withholding the funds. Harvard returned to the First Circuit on Tuesday for another showdown with a federal agency. This time it was with the Department of Homeland Security, which has sought to prevent Harvard from enrolling international students. Harvard also prevailed in that case last year. At issue is whether the administration can lawfully strip Harvard of federal funding and its ability to enroll international students, a fight that has emerged as a test of how far the White House can go in using the power of the federal government to pressure colleges to make changes it wants. The Trump administration used the cudgel of alleged antisemitism at Harvard to go after both its federal research funding and international student enrollment, arguing that the university didn’t sufficiently respond to Jewish students’ reports of discrimination. But on appeal, government lawyers focused on whether Burroughs had the authority to restore the funding. “When you look specifically at the grant terminations, there’s no First Amendment right to money,” Justice Department lawyer Michael K. Velchik told a panel of judges Monday. While Velchik accepted that federal district courts can hear Harvard’s First Amendment claims, he argued that the dispute over restoring terminated grants belonged in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims. Velchik’s argument hinged on the idea that restoring canceled research funding effectively amounted to enforcing federal contracts, which he said belonged in another court. But Harvard attorney Paul Clement told the panel of three judges that the university was seeking relief that could not be provided by the Court of Federal Claims. He dismissed the notion that the issue at hand is contractual, arguing that the case is about Harvard’s free speech rights. “These are not claims that really depend on the contract in any particular way,” Clement said. “They are claims to be free from retaliatory discrimination under the First Amendment.” Government attorneys also continued to argue this week that the Trump administration has the authority to withhold funds because—in its view—Harvard has not done enough to address antisemitism on campus. But the judges appeared unswayed by that argument. First Circuit Judge Sandra Lynch noted that the government acted against Harvard before proving claims of pervasive antisemitism on campus. (Separately, the Department of Justice sued Harvard in March over alleged antisemitism. A federal judge dismissed that case in August, finding the Trump administration had not demonstrated ongoing violations of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, a federal law that prohibits antisemitism.) “The claim is that Harvard has been indifferent to antisemitism; there are no findings, there was no investigation, there was simply an announcement: ‘We’re terminating,’ against that backdrop,” Lynch said. “It rather looks like the administration didn’t want to have to cope with what the law and the facts of the case presented under both Title VI and the Constitution [say].” She also questioned why the federal government did not use established Title VI processes to address concerns about alleged antisemitism at Harvard before taking punitive action. Lynch, a Clinton appointee, said that the federal government’s claims that Harvard discriminated against Jewish students and failed to adequately police antisemitism on campus are “the precise topics covered by Title VI.” Despite a prior legal setback, the Trump administration appears intent on blocking Harvard from enrolling international students, who comprise nearly a quarter of its student body, per university data. Trump’s proclamation that would have cut off international student enrollment at Harvard was blocked by Burroughs from taking effect in summer 2025 but also expired on its own in December. Justice Department lawyer Tiberius Davis said the federal government had held off on handing down a second order of the same nature because the judge’s order would prevent it from being enforced, but the idea is still in play. Now the White House is looking to revive the ban if the courts clear the way. “I can’t reveal exact conversations or with who, but I have been told by people with the White House that it’s likely he would reissue,” Davis said Tuesday. But First Circuit Judge Gustavo A. Gelpí, a Biden appointee, questioned how such a policy would eliminate antisemitism when it would also bar students from Israel from attending Harvard. title: Honda Reportedly Delays Production of the Next-Gen CR-V Hybrid Until April 2027 - Car and Driver
content: Next-generation CR-Vs will enter production three months late, but they’ll eventually take over the Civic’s spot in Honda’s Indiana plant. The Honda CR-V is getting a major redesign for 2028, but the automaker is reportedly pushing back the start of production to make more 2027 models first. Though the delayed start date means lower output of the new CR-V in the first year, Honda is clearing space for increased production in the near future, according to a report from Automotive News. The CR-V is Honda’s most popular nameplate in the United States, making up 9.5 percent of Honda’s total U.S. sales through September this year. The Civic comes in second place, but Honda is prioritizing U.S. production of the redesigned compact SUV over its economy car in 2028. See all results for new 2026 Honda CR-V Hybrid for sale near 23917 Last year, Honda shifted a lot of its CR-V production from Canada to the United States to lower the impact of import tariffs. U.S.-market CR-Vs are now primarily built in East Liberty, Ohio, and Greensburg, Indiana. The current-generation CR-Vs are in high demand, so Honda is reportedly pushing production of the redesigned hybrid-only CR-V to April 2027 to give this year’s model a bit more production time. The delay means Honda is said to be expecting a 6.7 percent decrease in its monthly output of the redesigned model in its first year. However, that reduction will be followed by a huge production increase. The AN report says Honda is canceling its original plans to build the next-gen Civic at its Indiana plant beginning in May 2028, which gives the CR-V plenty of breathing room once the Civic moves out. The Indiana plant is projected to build around 70,000 Civics this year. Civic hatchbacks sold in North America are exclusively built in Indiana. While the next-gen Civic sedan will still be built in Canada, Honda will begin importing Civic hatchbacks from its Japanese plant once next-gen production takes over. The restructuring is part of Honda’s ambitious plan to release 15 new or heavily refreshed models globally by 2030, with an emphasis on its next-generation hybrid powertrains. Honda is reportedly planning to build another hybrid-focused assembly plant in the United States, but that space is likely claimed by its upcoming large hybrid SUV lineup. The next-generation CR-V will reportedly be sold with only a hybrid powertrain and is projected to start production in 2027 for the 2028 model year. title: Wilmer's new glaucoma chief Thomas V. Johnson III on his vision - Ophthalmology Times
content: The Wilmer Eye Institute's new Glaucoma Division chief discusses mentoring junior faculty, multicenter trials, and optic nerve regeneration. Thomas V. Johnson III, MD, PhD, the Shelley and Allan Holt Rising Professor of Ophthalmology at the Wilmer Eye Institute at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine in Baltimore, Maryland, was recently named chief of the Glaucoma Division. He is the division’s third chief, following Harry A. Quigley, MD, and Pradeep Y. Ramulu, MD, MHS, PhD. In this Q&A with Ophthalmology Times (OT), Johnson discusses his vision for the role, including mentoring junior faculty and building infrastructure for multicenter clinical trials. He also reflects on how leading residents through the early COVID-19 pandemic shaped his approach to leadership, how his work founding a community vision screening program informs his view of access to care, and how close optic nerve regeneration is to reaching patients. Note: Transcript edited lightly for clarity and length. Thomas V. Johnson III, MD, PhD: Thank you very much! Fortunately, as the third chief of the Wilmer Glaucoma Division, I am standing on the shoulders of Drs. Harry Quigley and Pradeep Ramulu, who built and led this division for many years. Together, they did an incredible job of recruiting some of the best clinicians and scientists in our field and establishing a culture of clinical excellence, scholarly rigor, and collegiality that makes this an incredible place to spend a career. So, my top priority is simply to not break anything! Beyond that however, I have two major foci at present. First is to continue building the careers of our junior faculty, five of whom completed fellowship within the past few years. Thankfully, I anticipate that this will be an easy job since they are all outstanding glaucoma physicians and brilliant scientists who are already making important contributions to the research in our field. Second, I am working to increase our infrastructure to lead multicenter clinical trials. As a glaucoma specialist and a neuroscientist, I am incredibly excited by the neuroprotective therapies coming down the R&D pipeline and I want Wilmer Eye Institute to be at the forefront of this work in the coming years. Johnson: The ACS year at Wilmer Eye Institute is a transformational experience that not only provides an opportunity for service to the institution and education for our residents, but also a unique capacity for leadership development. I think this has borne out in the sheer number of former Wilmer ACSs who have gone on to become department Chairs, society/professional organization presidents, and other prominent leaders in our field. Peter J. McDonnell, MD, our department Chair, prioritizes leadership development for our trainees and faculty, and through that I’ve read a lot about leadership styles. The one that speaks to me most directly is Servant Leadership, wherein one leads by example and serves to empower and prioritize the growth of those they are leading. I really try to embody that ethos whenever I can, and my ACS year provided a unique opportunity for this with the initial surge of the COVID-19 pandemic. As many will recall, this was a scary time when exposure to infected patients was associated with real risk; the mortality rate was significant. Nonetheless, sick patients in our hospital had to be treated and if they had an eye problem, they needed to see an ophthalmologist. During the first few weeks of the pandemic, I didn’t feel it was reasonable to subject our residents to that uncertain risk if not necessary, so I saw all of the inpatient consults myself. Fortunately, Johns Hopkins adapted to the uncertainty very quickly and put clear protocols in place to ensure the safety of all the clinical staff, so the residents were able to get back to experiential learning rather quickly. But the experience helped instill in me a mentality that a leader shouldn’t ask anyone to do something that they wouldn’t readily do themselves. Johnson: Absolutely. We started the SightSavers program (now called the Vision Screening In Our Neighborhoods or ViSION Program) in 2011 and once again, I have to credit Harry Quigley with helping to make it happen. One of our founding tenets that we continue to adhere to today is that screening for eye disease is unhelpful unless it also provides a mechanism to clinically address newly discovered pathology. I am grateful that Wilmer Eye Institute has the capacity to care for patients regardless of their insurance status or ability to pay, through a generous, anonymous philanthropic gift that we lovingly refer to as the “Angel Fund.” Through that mechanism, the ViSION program and Wilmer Eye Institute Glaucoma Faculty have the ability not to worry about insurance reimbursement and instead focus on the care of the patients in our clinics and operating rooms. Putting the patient first has always been a central part of the Wilmer Eye Institute culture, and I certainly intend to continue fostering that mentality as glaucoma chief. Johnson: I am tremendously excited for the future of regenerative medicine in ophthalmology and in glaucoma specifically. While restoring vision to people who are blind from glaucoma through optic nerve regeneration has been a distant dream for decades, it is clear to me that neuroscience, stem cell biology, molecular biology, and biomedical engineering have advanced to the point that restoring lost sight will be possible. I think the scientific community is recognizing that, too, and the enthusiasm of the more than 300 international members of the RGC Repopulation, Stem Cell Transplantation, and Optic Nerve Regeneration (RReSTORe) Consortium underscores that point. In our own laboratories, we are now able to take human stem cell derived retinal ganglion cells, transplant them into the eyes of preclinical models of glaucoma, and observe not only functional (synaptic) connectivity in the retina but axonal growth through the optic nerve and into the brain. I think that full-length anterior visual pathway regeneration in animal models is just around the corner. That said, it is always challenging to predict how long this will take to translate to human patients, and a first-in-human clinical trial likely remains several years away. At this point, the biggest hurdle is going to be increasing the efficiency of RGC replacement from a few hundred neurons to tens of thousands—a number that will ultimately be required to restore a meaningful level of vision to patients blind from glaucoma and other optic neuropathies. Johnson: Continued success for the Wilmer Eye Institute glaucoma division will involve first and foremost, maintaining our leadership in clinical excellence, education, and vision research. Beyond that, I strive to continue mentoring and helping to build the careers of our junior faculty. For some, that will mean developing and growing a clinical and research program at Wilmer Eye Institute and for others that will mean taking on new leadership opportunities outside our institution. Indeed, while we were terribly sad for ourselves to see Pradeep Ramulu move to become the Chair at Bascom Palmer Eye Institute, we also recognize that such a transition to a prominent leadership role is exactly what our institution and our glaucoma division are all about: cultivating and building clinical, educational, research, and leadership excellence so that we can impact our field beyond the walls of our own institution. title: The Big Idea: Mia V. Moss - John Scalzi's Whatever
content:
Posted on			October 7, 2026
			  
			Posted by			Athena Scalzi							  
				  
				2 Comments A lot can happen when you take a one-thousand year nap, and there may or may not be consequences when you wake up. Author Mia V. Moss takes an interesting look at false narratives and wrongfully upheld beliefs in the Big Idea for her newest novel, The Heresy of Thieves. Humans are story-powered creatures. We tell stories about the stars, the seasons, ourselves, and each other. And if we are very rich or persuasive in other ways, the stories we tell about others are the stories that get labeled ‘reality,’ whether the subject of the story agrees with that label or not. Sometimes the labels our fellow humans foist upon us are benign. Sometimes you say “oh that’s a cute chicken figurine” to a relative as you window shop at the mall. And then forever after at Christmas you are The One Who Loves Chickens and are gifted yet another chicken figurine from a beaming well-intentioned relative, who is very proud of their talent for gift-giving. Then there is the 1995 romcom, While You Were Sleeping. Peter, the man we believe to be the romantic male lead, spends most of the film in a coma. We are informed at the beginning of the film by the female lead, Sandra Bullock’s Lucy, that Peter is perfect. He is a rich, handsome, kind, charming, rich lawyer in Chicago. Peter has a freaking newspaper clipping of the time when, as a boy, he saved a nest of baby squirrels that had fallen from a tree! Peter is a sexy saint, genetically engineered to be Lucy’s soul mate. Except, by the end of the film (spoilers, sorry) we know that Peter’s life is a hollow pretense. He has a girlfriend who he cheats on. He lives alone with no pets. He hardly ever makes time in his life for the people who care about him. He knocked the baby squirrels out of the nest on purpose with a rock and simply did not correct the adults when they cobbled together a story that he had rescued them and took his picture for the paper! He is no hero at all and certainly not good enough for Sandra Bullock. So, when I set out to write The Heresy of Thieves, my big idea was this: what if the story people formed about you ended up creating a religion? Not really novel, considering exhibit A: Christianity. But what if the person they formed a religion around had no idea this had happened? What if they were really pissed, in fact, to find out about all the stuff done in their name? And what if, by giving that person their agency back, the rest of society immediately crumbled to ruin? The concept and exploration of those consequences branches out from my overarching conceit of the Spellfall trilogy: what if two powerful entities in the midst of a messy, centuries-long mage war just wanted to remove themselves from all of the murder and dynastic backbiting and make out in a nice backyard garden for eternity instead? Much of the book’s revisions took place during the earlier years of the COVID-19 pandemic. I watched as the US government changed the story of health and safety measures to suit corporate needs, and observed how people accepted or rejected those truths. How quickly official health messaging morphed from ‘masks are an essential and widely accepted way to mitigate the spread of airborne disease’ to ‘wearing a mask is for cowards.’ It was fascinating to observe that it takes hardly any time at all for a person with a wide enough reach to sculpt bespoke truths for a whole society. This, then, became a much larger focus of the book, and served to strengthen what I had first set out to accomplish with Vael. Vael being both the event that drives the narrative of the first book and the main character of the series. The stories people tell of you can shape your life in ways you may not fully understand at first. Maybe, like Vael, you sneak away from The War to have a good snog with your divine lover and then wake up a thousand years later to learn the prosperous functioning of the entire realm relies on you never waking up and people are going to be righteously pissed if they find out you don’t want to do that. Maybe, like Peter, you get caught knocking squirrels out of nests by a passing reporter and then build a hollow life for yourself as an adult in an attempt to shield your psyche from the crushing guilt every time your family displays the framed newspaper article. Maybe you wake up one day, surrounded by chicken statues in a too small apartment, and wonder what you could have done to prevent a timeline where you might one day be buried in feathery bric-a-brac from the Hallmark store. It’s me, I’m chickens statues. Please stop gifting me chickens, I’m begging you. But if you must, and I do perish beneath their cute ceramic wings, can we at least agree that you won’t turn it into some sort of foundational story for a new religion? The Heresy of Thieves: Amazon|Barnes & Noble|Bookshop|Green Apple Books Added to my list — maybe you could re-home the chickens? Every time I wake up from a nap, it feels like a thousand-year nap. title: The Arguments We Did and Didn’t Hear in Suncor v. Boulder - Legal Planet
content: The Supreme Court heard oral arguments today in Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County. At issue is whether the city and county of Boulder can move forward with its state court case against defendants Exxon Mobil Corporation and Suncor Energy for allegedly deceiving the public about their products’ role in climate change. Some three dozen local governments and states throughout the United States have filed similar lawsuits in state court against fossil fuel companies over their alleged deception and false advertising. Although none of these cases have yet gone to trial, the U.S. Supreme Court decided to review Boulder’s case at the request of the oil company petitioners. There is much to unpack about the arguments and how the justices received them. But I first want to highlight an argument that went largely unmade, one that may matter as the justices decide the case. (You can read or hear the arguments at the court’s website.) Several justices pressed the idea that a tort suit is regulation by another name. Justice Barrett put it most directly: “Everybody agrees that state tort law is a form of regulation.” Justice Kavanaugh warned that suits like Boulder’s could “bankrupt” defendants. Chief Justice Roberts asked whether the suit was “an attempt to evade” the Court’s precedents on emissions. Boulder’s counsel answered that a damages award doesn’t prohibit anything; it just requires defendants “to internalize a portion of the cost of their activities.” That is true. But it invites a response the Court has given before: damages regulate conduct too. There’s another answer: The Supreme Court has always recognized that tort verdicts influence behavior, and it has never treated that as a reason to wipe out state remedies Congress chose to preserve. That’s why, as I told Mother Jones in a preview article, it’s useful to see Suncor as a tort case rather than as a climate lawsuit. From nuclear power to tobacco to pesticides, the Court has held that federal regulation and state compensation can coexist. I’ll expound on my reasoning below. First, let’s turn to what was actually argued. The oil companies’ broadest theory had a bad day, but narrower ones are very much alive. Several justices resisted the idea that the Constitution’s structure alone bars state climate suits. Justice Kagan asked of the companies’ “plan of the Convention” theory: “Where’s the text for that? Where’s the support for that? Where’s the precedent for that? Where’s the anything for that?” Justice Barrett called the companies’ retreat to constitutional structure “a little slippery.” Justices Gorsuch, Sotomayor, and Jackson also pressed hard on it. The first was Justice Kavanaugh’s. In his view, four precedents (Milwaukee I, Milwaukee II, International Paper Co. v. Ouellette, and American Electric Power v. Connecticut, or AEP) make “crystal-clear that interstate air and water pollution are matters for federal law unless Congress specifically preserves state law.” On that reading, the Clean Air Act preserves suits under the law of the state where the pollution originates (the “source state”). It does not preserve suits under the law of the injured state, like Colorado. When petitioners’ counsel pointed out that Boulder is relying on Colorado law, Kavanaugh replied, “That resolves this case.” The second was Justice Kagan’s. She pointed to AEP’s closing paragraph, which says that whether a state suit is available depends on the preemptive effect of the Clean Air Act. That makes this an ordinary question of statutory preemption, not constitutional structure. But Kagan also suggested to Boulder’s counsel that the Clean Air Act might be “the more natural and simpler route towards [the companies’] view of what should happen here.” So, both narrower routes could still limit the options for Boulder. The open question is how much of the case survives. It’s worth noting that the foreign-affairs framing that dominated op-ed pages in the lead-up to argument drew no questions from the justices. It came up only in petitioners’ opening and, briefly, in rebuttal. So, what can we tell from the questions each justice asked? Justices Sotomayor and Jackson: seem firmly with Boulder. Sotomayor: (1) noted the companies hadn’t raised their extraterritoriality argument below until their reply brief; (2) questioned the Court’s jurisdiction, and asked whether it should certify the question of Colorado procedure to the Colorado Supreme Court rather than decide it; (3) said she didn’t know that “we’ve ever talked of spending money on litigation as a constitutional injury”; (4) told Boulder’s counsel that this case looks like Commonwealth Edison v. Montana, which upheld a state coal tax despite the Clean Air Act: “Isn’t this your case?” Jackson called the case premature, noting the companies’ other federal defenses are still pending in state court. She said the companies’ extraterritoriality test “seems very close to a causation standard” and asked why they were trying to “constitutionalize” it. She also asked the Principal Deputy Solicitor General, Sarah Harris, whether Colorado, home to Suncor’s refineries, is itself a source state. That question matters, because Ouellette preserves source-state law. Justice Kavanaugh: firmly with the oil companies. He nearly coached the Solicitor General’s office toward a stronger argument: interstate pollution is federal unless Congress preserves state law, so why wasn’t that the lead? He answered Kagan’s tobacco-and-opioids question by saying air and water pollution are different. He asked why a tort suit should be treated differently from a state statute doing the same thing. He closed by quoting AEP’s line that an expert agency is better equipped than “individual district judges” to address climate change, and asked whether the same isn’t true of “a six-person state jury in Boulder.” Justice Barrett: leaning toward the companies, but by a narrower route. She rejected the companies’ constitutional-structure theory. She read the Clean Air Act’s savings clauses as preserving, not authorizing, preexisting state authority: “It says ‘preserve.’ And a saving clause suggests that you’re saving something that already exists.” But she described that preexisting state authority as “much more circumscribed.” She agreed the Clean Air Act did not make state law “spring into effect.” And she embraced Kavanaugh’s framing: “I think Justice Kavanaugh is right. It’s also simply in our precedent. We’ve called it an enclave of federal common law.” To Boulder, she posed a hypothetical Colorado statute capping emissions in the other 49 states. When Boulder’s counsel agreed such a statute would be invalid, she asked: “So, the same thing can happen through the tort suit, though?” Barrett also raised EPA’s recent position that the Clean Air Act does not authorize regulating greenhouse gases from motor vehicles. Her point was not that this helps Boulder. If the Act no longer displaces federal common law, she suggested, the issue reverts to federal common law, and a federal court could decide there is no cause of action. She seems prepared to rule for the companies without their constitutional theory. Justice Kagan: with Boulder on method, uncertain on outcome. She pressed the companies hardest. She noted the suit resembles the 1990s tobacco suits and the more recent opioid litigation: “This is chapter 3. So, if this is chapter 3, were chapters 1 and 2 also preempted?” She added that the companies may have a weaker claim on the merits, “but this is the same kind of lawsuit against the same kind of actors for the same kind of harm.” She also challenged the constitutional theory and pointed to AEP’s closing paragraph. With Boulder’s counsel, though, she asked: “You really read Milwaukee I to allow state regulation of air and water to any significant degree?” She also said Boulder’s suits “are so related to what kinds of emissions are appropriate.” When Boulder’s counsel argued that EPA’s disclaimer of authority makes Clean Air Act preemption hard to decide, she replied that “the statute is the statute.” Her tobacco analogy suggests sympathy for the deception claims. Her Clean Air Act questions suggest skepticism about claims based on production and emissions. One shouldn’t count her as a vote to keep every claim. Justice Gorsuch: seems skeptical of the companies’ theory, but hard to read. His Texas hypothetical exposed a gap in petitioners’ logic: they would object even to Texas law applied to a Texas source. He then pressed the Solicitor General’s office. EPA, he noted, has disclaimed the power to regulate greenhouse gases “not just from motor vehicles but more recently from stationary sources too.” If the Clean Air Act displaced federal common law and state law is also barred, “nobody can sue at all?” Harris answered, “I think that’s correct.” That skepticism fits Gorsuch’s opinions in National Pork Producers v. Ross and Virginia Uranium. He asked Boulder’s counsel whether this is “the same thing as the classic car manufacturer case.” Chief Justice Roberts: seems skeptical of both sides, and harder on Boulder by the end. He pressed petitioners’ counsel with an ordinary tort hypothetical: if you throw a rock over the border and hit someone, you can be sued there. He told the Solicitor General’s office that familiar mass-tort and internet cases seem to be “precisely what’s going on here.” But with Boulder’s counsel, he raised the prospect of municipalities in every state copying Boulder’s pleadings. He then asked, “isn’t your suit an attempt to evade those decisions? It’s really … an effort to reduce emissions.” Justice Thomas: uncertain but may be leaning toward the companies on the merits. He opened both petitioners’ and the government’s arguments by asking about jurisdiction, but he often opens that way, so I wouldn’t read much into it. More telling, he asked Boulder’s counsel whether anything limits whom plaintiffs can sue, including large retailers. Counsel acknowledged, “Nothing in our theory prevents that.” Since our previous Legal Planet Guide offered possible outcomes—always speculative, of course—here’s how it looks after oral arguments, roughly from most to least likely: As I said at the outset, Justice Barrett is right in one sense: “everybody agrees” tort law regulates, even if it is intended to address actual harms not addressed by statutes. However, the Court has never treated a tort remedy’s regulatory effect, by itself, as a reason to preempt it. Here’s my reasoning: That’s my take. What did you think? Share in the comments.
